Chapter 27

Two layouts and a group

A root layout with view transitions and a progress bar; an (app) group layout with the header, $state.eager for the current link, the new-version banner, and the artist’s name from a remote query; plus the small pieces every page uses.

By the end of this chapter

Know what a layout group is and why the embed demo escapes it; use onNavigate for a view transition that never holds a navigation hostage; and reach for $state.eager when async Svelte holds a value back that should not wait.

The root layout is deliberately almost empty: the stylesheet, the view transitions, a progress bar. The header lives one level down, in (app)/+layout.svelte. The parentheses make (app) a *layout group* — a folder that adds a layout without adding a segment to the URL — and the one page that must have no header, the embed demo that pretends to be somebody else’s site, resets to the root with a +page@.svelte.

The first check is new with SvelteKit 3. A shallow navigation — a panel opening in the studio (ch. 18), a preview in the gallery (ch. 30) — now runs onNavigate like any other, and it changes history rather than the document, so navigation.shallow returns before a cross-fade can start; the panel brings its own transition. Then the two guards the comment names — no API, or a person who asked for reduced motion, means no transition — and one it does not: a tab that is not visible has nobody to cross-fade for.

Why the transition has a timeout

onNavigate returns a promise SvelteKit waits for before completing the navigation. Wrapping it in startViewTransition hands the browser both states of the page and lets it cross-fade. But a transition must never hold a navigation hostage: the promise resolves when the update callback runs, or when the transition reports it cannot start, or after three hundred milliseconds — whichever is first. While chasing a flaky back navigation this guard was the first suspect and was innocent (the cause was forkPreloads, ch. 38); it stayed because it rules out a whole class of hang for nothing.

The app layout

Why every internal link is resolve()

A link written as a string — href="/jam/lobby", or "/p/" with an id glued on — is checked by nothing. Rename the p/[id] folder and every one of them still compiles, and every one of them is a 404 in production. resolve() from $app/paths takes a route *id* — "/(app)/jam/[room]", layout group and all — and its parameters, and the route table generated by svelte-kit sync types both: a misspelt id or a missing parameter is a type error. It also prefixes the base path, if the app is ever served under one. Search and hash ride along on the id, resolve("/(app)/gallery#yours"), and the server uses the same function for a redirect (ch. 24). ESLint’s svelte/no-navigation-without-resolve holds the line, and is on for the whole app; the few navigations with nothing to resolve — goto(""), the reload banner below, a blob: download, a vanity address, which is not a route until reroute makes it one — say so on the line, and the one folder it is off for is the embeddable player, which runs on pages where there is no SvelteKit at all (ch. 33). With paths.relative: false (ch. 2) the server writes the same /studio the browser would, which is what lets aria-current below compare a resolved link with page.url.pathname.

Why $state.eager

With async Svelte, a navigation’s state changes are held back until the new page’s awaits resolve, so the interface never shows half an update. That is right for content and wrong for the thing somebody just clicked: a nav link that stays un-highlighted for the four hundred milliseconds a remote query takes feels broken. $state.eager(pathname) reads the *incoming* value immediately — for this one attribute and nothing else. The rest of the page still waits.

version.pollInterval in the config makes SvelteKit check for a new build every minute and set updated.current when it finds one. Client-side navigation would then ask for JavaScript files that no longer exist, so beforeNavigate turns the next navigation into a full page load — unless it is shallow, because a shallow navigation never asks the server for a file and a new deployment is no reason to reload the studio under a panel that is opening. The banner gives the person the choice to do that now; the hook makes sure it happens anyway. data-sveltekit-reload on the link is what makes it a real reload rather than a client-side navigation, and the link is the one href in the app with nothing to resolve() — it is the address already in the bar — so the line above it tells the linter so. The banner’s fly asks prefersReducedMotion for its duration: a Svelte transition runs on the Web Animations API, which the stylesheet’s reduced-motion rule cannot reach.

Who this browser is comes from whoAmI(), a remote query, rather than from layout data. The forms that change the answer call whoAmI().refresh() in their handlers (ch. 24), and the new value arrives in the same response as the submission. A layout load would have needed a second round trip to notice — and in an earlier version of this project, it did, and the header showed the old name until the next navigation.

A handle may be twenty characters, and on a phone, after the logo and four links, the header has room for only part of one. Without min-width: 0, a flex item will not shrink below its content: the chip held its full width, the header grew past the screen, and the whole page could be dragged sideways. The links already scroll inside their own list — that only works once the <nav> is allowed to be narrower than they are — and the handle is cut short with an ellipsis, with the whole of it in title, and given its full width again from 40rem up. Mobile first again: the phone is the case the rules are written for, and the wide screen is the one that relaxes them. The end-to-end suite found this the hard way, and now checks it directly with the longest handle there can be (ch. 38).

The small pieces

<svelte:element this={...}> renders whichever tag the string names, so one component is an h2 on the landing page and an h3 inside a panel, and the document outline — what a screen reader navigates by — stays honest.

toast("Saved") from anywhere — an event handler, a catch block — with no <Toasts /> host to remember. mount creates a component at a target, unmount removes it, and { outro: true } lets its transition:fly play on the way out. These are the same two functions SvelteKit itself uses to start the app.

With SvelteKit 3 the error page is a real <svelte:boundary> around the page below it, on the server as well as the client: a component that throws while rendering lands here rather than taking the whole response down. What it shows is its error prop, typed by the generated ErrorProps as App.Error — and since SvelteKit 3 an App.Error always carries status beside message, so the page needs nothing from $app/state. (It used to read page.error and page.status, which say the same thing less directly.) error.id is the correlation id handleError adds for unknown errors (ch. 26) — and src/error.html is the page for when even this cannot render.

Checkpoint

  • You can say what (app) does to the URL, and what +page@.svelte does to the layout chain.
  • You can explain when $state.eager is the right tool and when it would be wrong.
  • You can trace what happens on the first navigation after a deploy.
